analysis.one_liner: Allows pharmacists and wholesalers to import cheaper FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 56 House members including 55 Democrats and 1 Republican, sat in a subcommittee without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write rules letting licensed pharmacists and wholesalers import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada, where the same medicines sell for far less. It would also have barred drug makers from cutting off or discriminating against pharmacies that import, and let individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply with a valid prescription. It was introduced by Rep. Bernie Sanders in April 2002 and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs, especially seniors and the uninsured, who could have bought FDA-approved medicines at Canadian prices. Licensed US pharmacies and wholesalers would have gained a legal channel to buy cheaper drugs abroad, and individual patients would have gotten clear legal protection to import a 90-day personal supply.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write regulations allowing licensed pharmacists and wholesalers to import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada, opening a legal channel to buy medicines at Canadian prices.

Makes it unlawful for drug manufacturers to discriminate against pharmacies or wholesalers that import, including by limiting supply or offering worse terms than they give foreign buyers — a direct response to the industry practice of cutting off pharmacies that reimport.

Lets individuals import up to a 90-day supply of an FDA-approved drug from a registered Canadian seller with a valid prescription, and directs regulators to focus enforcement on imports that pose a real health threat rather than on personal-use purchases.

Includes anti-counterfeit safeguards: importers must test each batch for authenticity and degradation at approved labs, document the drug's chain of custody back to the manufacturer, and register with regulators, with immediate suspension powers if a pattern of counterfeits appears.
Orders the Comptroller General to report within 18 months on how the policy affected retail drug prices, and the Institute of Medicine to study whether imports were counterfeit or unsafe.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, in the form of cheaper Canadian competition in the US market and a ban on the supply limits and discriminatory terms they used to protect US prices. The FDA and regulators would also take on new certification, registration, and enforcement work, funded by appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have added counterfeit and adulterated drugs to the US supply if testing and chain-of-custody safeguards failed; the bill itself acknowledges this risk by requiring batch-by-batch authenticity testing, lab certification of every shipment, and immediate suspension powers, and critics argued no paperwork regime could fully guarantee foreign supply chains.

Savings were not guaranteed: the bill does not force manufacturers to lower US prices, so benefits depended on pharmacies actually using the import channel and on enforcement of the anti-discrimination rule against supply limits, which manufacturers could contest in court.
Drug makers argued that cheaper reimportation would cut their US revenues and therefore the investment they fund into new drug research; the bill does not address this tradeoff.
The documentation, testing, and registration requirements would impose compliance costs on pharmacies, wholesalers, and Canadian sellers, which could shrink the savings passed to patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large and direct: Americans pay some of the highest drug prices in the world for identical FDA-approved products sold for less across the border, and this bill attacked that gap through a tested channel with layered anti-counterfeit safeguards. The real risks are safety and design: a paper-based testing regime can fail, savings depend on importers actually gaining access, and manufacturers would have fought the anti-discrimination rule. On balance, the bill's benefits to people paying drug prices outweigh its costs, but it was a narrower fix than measures that directly lower US prices, and its safety regime added real administrative weight.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House committee and then to a health subcommittee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on April 25, 2002, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
Within two weeks, on May 6, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where the committee record ends.

The bill attracted 56 cosponsors — 55 of 208 House Democrats and 1 of 223 House Republicans — but never received a markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

Because no vote ever happened, the bill never became law, and commercial importation of prescription drugs from Canada remained illegal; the measure was not reintroduced to completion in this Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: with the bill dying in subcommittee, they kept the US market closed to cheaper Canadian imports and continued charging Americans more than Canadians for the same FDA-approved drugs.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.role: Sponsor, at-large House member from Vermont
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permit commercial drug importation from Canada and assembled a broad cosponsor list.

for.name: 1 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it token crossover support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and referred it to the Subcommittee on Health without scheduling a markup or vote; no further action appears in the record.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of jurisdiction, never brought the bill to a markup or floor vote; he later became the top lobbyist for the pharmaceutical industry's trade group.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed reimportation legislation, arguing it threatened drug safety and industry revenue, and worked to keep such bills from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 55 of 208 House Democrats versus 1 of 223 House Republicans — and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill, though no vote occurred to measure the split directly.

industries.note: The bill would have opened the US market to the same FDA-approved drugs sold for less in Canada and barred the supply limits and discriminatory terms manufacturers use to keep US prices high. Its defeat preserved the price gap that makes US prescription drug costs the highest in the world.

Licensed pharmacists and wholesalers would have gained a legal right to buy FDA-approved drugs from registered Canadian sellers, with labeling and testing rules, letting them pass savings to patients.
Canadian sellers registered with US regulators would have gained a large new export market for prescription drugs destined for American patients.
